clue.text: Policeman having a threesome beginning to titillate fellow citizen

parts.note: cop is the everyday word for a policeman

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is the letter it starts on, so only that opening letter of what follows is taken.

parts.note: the clue's own word, taken as it stands
a trio is three of anything together
the first letter of that word, and nothing else of it

explanation.surface: A policeman who has joined a threesome and is beginning to enjoy himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The four pieces cut clean across the word's own seams: nothing in the clue points at the prefix co- or at the patriot behind it. 'Beginning to titillate' reads as part of the scene and is worth one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Co- means alongside, so the word names the patriot alongside you — somebody who shares your country, which is a fellow citizen.

clue.text: Message bishop wearing lace pants

indicators.note: the lace goes around the bishop as if he had it on, so the letter sits inside
pants as an adjective is British slang for rubbish, so the lace is poor and its letters are muddled

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A cleric caught in lacy underwear, a story for a telegram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear but is British slang for rubbish, signalling that LACE is jumbled; 'wearing' puts B inside the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable is a telegram, an old-fashioned message sent by wire.

clue.text: Spooner's sexy apostle is in difficulty

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words here change places

parts.note: fit is British slang for sexy; with the opening sounds traded it is said as a hole in the ground
Paul is the apostle; with the opening sounds traded it is said as a tumble

explanation.surface: An attractive saint finds himself in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' trades the opening sounds of FIT PAUL, so it is heard as PIT FALL; fit is British slang for physically attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitfall is a hidden danger or snag, so a source of difficulty.

clue.text: God, Norse, shows spine

parts.note: the hammer-wielding god of Norse myth
n is the label a dictionary puts on a word of Norse origin

explanation.surface: A Norse god showing some backbone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norse' is asked to work twice over: it tells you which god is wanted, then hands over a letter of its own. The definition is botanical, not anatomical.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a spine is the sharp woody point on a stem, which is what a thorn is on a rose or a blackthorn.

clue.text: Begin perhaps boosting current king? Yes, in Madrid

indicators.note: To boost a thing is to push it upwards, and in a down clue what goes up is read from the foot of the entry back to the top.

parts.note: i is the symbol for electric current in a physics formula
Shakespeare's Lear, the king who split his kingdom between his daughters
si is yes in Spanish, and Madrid is named to point at the language

explanation.surface: Somebody in Madrid agreeing that the present king should be talked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Menachem Begin was prime minister of Israel, and 'perhaps' warns that the name is one instance of the answer rather than a synonym for it. 'Current' is the physicist's I, the letter on the other side of Ohm's law from the voltage.
explanation.definitionFit: Menachem Begin, who signed the Camp David accords as prime minister, was Israeli, so the name stands as one example of the nationality.

clue.text: Setter confused over Unionist politician's memorial for the fallen?

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above what follows
the setter is muddled, so the word's letters are jumbled

parts.note: MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A puzzled crossword setter writing about a Unionist politician's war memorial.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals the joke: a stump is what remains to remember a felled tree by, not a war memorial.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree stump is all that marks where a felled tree stood, a whimsical monument to it.

clue.text: Perhaps something in miniscule fragment of pretty pottery

indicators.note: A fragment is a piece broken out of something bigger, so what is wanted is a short unbroken run inside the words that follow.

parts.note: four letters in an unbroken run, starting inside the first word and stopping inside the second

explanation.surface: Something small spotted in a chip of pretty pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miniscule' is spelt wrong on purpose — minuscule is the word — so the definition is pointing at the clue's own fourth word. The rest of the sentence is a hiding place, and 'fragment of' marks it.
explanation.definitionFit: A typo is a slip of the keyboard, and the clue's own 'miniscule' is one, so the definition names itself rather than describing anything else.

clue.text: Combined, like some soup containing whiskey?

indicators.note: A tin containing soup has the soup inside it, so the letter named after this word goes within the letters before.

parts.note: soup out of a tin is tinned soup
whiskey is W in the radio alphabet that starts Alpha, Bravo, Charlie

explanation.surface: Soup out of a tin with a slug of whiskey stirred into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Whiskey with an e is the radio alphabet's spelling, and that is the flag that one letter is wanted rather than a drink. The definition wants the participle two paired-off towns share.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things twinned are joined as a matching pair — as a British town is with one abroad — which is combined in the sense of yoked together.

clue.text: Pregnancy hormone for good developing isn't blocked by drug

indicators.note: A developing situation is one still changing shape, so the letters it touches settle into a different order.

parts.note: somebody for a proposal is pro it

indicators.note: A road blocked by a lorry has the lorry sitting in the middle of it, so the letter named goes in among the letters before.

parts.note: g is good on a school report
anagram fodder, four letters
e is ecstasy, the drug of a dance floor, and it joins the shuffle

explanation.surface: A hormone keeping a pregnancy safely on course even when a drug is taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For good' reads as permanently and is two separate pieces of wordplay. The answer is the manufactured form of progesterone, so the definition and the surface are talking about much the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A progestin is a synthetic progestogen, the hormone that keeps the womb lining ready for an embryo, so 'pregnancy hormone' names it by its job.

clue.text: Austria hit by disorder returning in killers' domain

parts.note: A is the international vehicle code for Austria
to bat is to hit

indicators.note: returning means the word for disorder is read backwards

parts.note: a riot is public disorder

explanation.surface: Austria troubled by unrest coming back, in a place where murderers rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit by' places the word for hit after A rather than signalling a blow; the killers are slaughtermen, not murderers.
explanation.definitionFit: An abattoir is a slaughterhouse, where animals are killed, so the slaughterers' territory.

clue.text: Journalist's stream over, over, over at last

indicators.note: over here means turned over, so the word for stream is read backwards

parts.note: a tide is a stream or current of water
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word over is taken

parts.note: the third over supplies its own final letter

explanation.surface: A reporter's river, repeated over and over, seems to be finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The three overs do three jobs: the first gives O, the second reverses TIDE, and the third supplies its own last letter R.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is a senior newspaper journalist who decides what gets printed.

clue.text: Get back American trapped in African country undergoing revolution

indicators.note: Somebody trapped in a place cannot get out of it, so the letter named before goes inside the word that follows.
A revolution turns a thing full circle, so the letters assembled are read from the end back to the start.

parts.note: Niger is the landlocked state on the southern edge of the Sahara
A is the standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An American held hostage in an African country in the middle of a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undergoing revolution' is the country's politics in the surface and an instruction to read backwards in the wordplay. Niger and Nigeria are two separate countries, both named for the river that runs through them.
explanation.definitionFit: To regain a thing is to get it back after losing it — a title, your breath, your composure — so the two verbs match sense and tense.

clue.text: Concentrates, being caught going in 3 directions, some more than once

indicators.note: What goes in ends up inside, so the letter named before it is written within the letters that follow.

parts.note: east, south and north as their single letters, east and south each used more than once: E, S, S, E, N, E, S
c is caught on a cricket scorecard, the way a batsman's dismissal is written

explanation.surface: Somebody caught heading off in three directions, more than once.
explanation.walkthrough: The 3 is the number itself rather than a pointer to another clue, and the directions are compass points shrunk to single letters. 'Some more than once' is the licence to use two of them again.
explanation.definitionFit: An essence is the concentrated extract of a plant — vanilla essence, essence of rose — so the plural is concentrates in a cook's sense.

clue.text: Confused tot supervised

parts.note: to tot up a column of figures is to add it
whoever supervised a party led it

explanation.surface: A muddled toddler being looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' is the verb, totting up a bill, rather than the small child the rest of the sentence wants. Both pieces are past tense, which keeps them in step with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An addled brain cannot think straight, the word having started out meaning rotten, as an addled egg is, so it is confused as an adjective.

clue.text: Haggard book, perhaps, is something from the sewer?

indicators.note: 'Perhaps' flags an example, so the word before it stands for the wider class it belongs to rather than for itself.

parts.note: a haggard face is a drawn one, tight and tired
a book is one of an author's works

explanation.surface: A Rider Haggard novel dredged up out of a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: The sewer is one who sews, not the drain, and the question mark is the only warning of it. Rider Haggard wrote King Solomon's Mines, which is why 'Haggard book' reads as a title rather than two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawn work is the openwork embroidery made by pulling threads out of a cloth, so it does come from a sewer in the needle-and-thread sense.

clue.text: Maybe loon meets chap following a different path

indicators.note: 'Maybe' flags an example, so the bird named after it is one instance of the wider word wanted.

parts.note: the waterbird North America calls a loon is the diver in Britain
a gent is a chap, the gentleman of a lavatory door cut short

explanation.surface: A lunatic running into a man who has taken another route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loon' is the bird rather than the lunatic the surface offers, and the British name for it is the piece wanted. 'Following' looks like a positional instruction and is part of the definition instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Divergent paths are ones that separate and head off at their own angles, so anything divergent is following a different path.

clue.text: Overwhelm single lady with vow of chastity at romantic encounter

parts.note: i is one in Roman numerals, and a single thing is one
a nun takes vows of poverty, chastity and obedience when she enters her order
an evening out with somebody you are courting is a date

explanation.surface: A single woman who has sworn off sex turning up for a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' is the numeral one, not the marital status the rest of the sentence pushes. The definition goes back to a Latin word for flooding, which is why it suits a river as readily as a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To inundate somebody is to flood them, with water or with letters and requests, which is to overwhelm them.

clue.text: Chinese right-wing politician initially regrets the result of over-indulging

parts.note: the Han are China's majority people, named after the dynasty
Michael Gove, the Conservative minister who ran the Cabinet Office and then edited The Spectator

indicators.note: What is done initially is done first, so only the first letter of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of that word, and nothing else of it

explanation.surface: A right-wing Chinese politician regretting what he drank last night.
explanation.walkthrough: Gove is the Conservative crosswords reach for when four letters of right-wing politician are wanted. 'Initially' attaches to the word after it rather than to the politician, which is where the final letter comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the headache and nausea of the morning after too much drink, which is the result of over-indulging in its plainest form.

clue.text: More magnificent kitchen implement picked up

indicators.note: Something picked up is overheard rather than read, so what counts is the noise the word makes.

parts.note: the tool you shred cheese on is a grater, and said aloud it is indistinguishable from the word wanted

explanation.surface: A finer kitchen gadget being lifted off the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' means overheard rather than lifted, and it is the only instruction in the clue. The two spellings sound alike because 'ea' and 'a' both come out as the long a of plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Greater is the comparative of great, so a greater hall or a greater name is the more magnificent one of two.

clue.text: Got better recipe combined

parts.note: R is the recipe at the head of a prescription, Latin for 'take', still written on a doctor's pad
nations combined against an enemy are allied

explanation.surface: Somebody who has ended up with a better recipe by putting two together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recipe' is the prescription abbreviation rather than the cookery sense the surface offers. The definition is a patient's recovery or a share price's, both of them in the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: A patient rallies and so does a market, meaning each recovers, so the past tense of that verb is 'got better'.

clue.text: Favourite pupil welcoming and unusually academic

indicators.note: the outer word takes the other in, so its letters go inside

parts.note: the teacher's pet is a favourite pupil

indicators.note: the word and appears in an unusual order, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A teacher's favourite student, friendly and remarkably scholarly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' looks like it modifies academic, but it jumbles AND into DAN, which PET welcomes.
explanation.definitionFit: Academic can mean overly concerned with theory and fine detail, which is exactly what a pedant is.

clue.text: Beasts of burden put on islands

parts.note: to don a coat is to put it on
the low coral islands strung out from the tip of Florida are the Keys

explanation.surface: Pack animals being put ashore on some islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' is the dressing verb, the one that goes with a hat, rather than anything to do with loading a cargo. The Keys take their name from cayo, the Spanish for a sandy islet.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey carries panniers and packs where no cart can go, which is what makes it the beast of burden of the phrase.

clue.text: Constituent of popular Tory leader with substantial backing

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Tory

indicators.note: backing means the word for substantial is read backwards

parts.note: large means substantial

explanation.surface: A popular Conservative leader with considerable support from his party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like political support but signals that LARGE is read in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral means forming a necessary part of a whole, as a constituent is.

clue.text: Rich, like lamb sauce?

definitions.meaning: the British slang sense of being rolling in money
mint sauce is what British cooking puts beside roast lamb, so that sauce is flavoured this way

explanation.surface: A sauce for lamb with something rich about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma does all the hiding: it reads as a comparison and it is really the join between two separate definitions. The money sense comes from coins being minted.
explanation.definitionFit: Minted is British slang for rolling in money, and the sauce served with roast lamb is mint sauce, so it is minted in the kitchen sense.

clue.text: Slogan of TV comedy originally ignored, then taken up

indicators.note: What is ignored is left out, and a word's original letter is the one it starts on, so that opening letter never gets written.
In a down clue taking something up reads it from the foot of the entry towards the top, so those letters run backwards.

parts.note: Bottom was the BBC sitcom of the early nineties with Rik Mayall and Adrian Edmondson sharing a squalid flat
the letter the sitcom's name starts on, dropped before anything else happens

explanation.surface: A comedy catchphrase nobody noticed at first that later caught on.
explanation.walkthrough: The comedy is Bottom, three series of two flatmates knocking each other about, and the clue turns entirely on knowing the title. 'Then' marks the order of the two operations, with the letter going before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is the short phrase a school or a family lives by, which is a slogan in its formal, carved-over-the-door form.

clue.text: Delighted if your hosts strengthen spiritually

indicators.note: A host has guests staying inside the house, so the words before this one have the letters wanted sitting within them.

parts.note: five letters in an unbroken run, starting inside the first word and stopping inside the last

explanation.surface: Delight at the people putting you up for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts late in the first word and stops early in the last, which is what keeps it out of sight. The definition is the church's sense of building somebody up, the Latin for 'build' sitting inside the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To edify is to build a person up morally — the word is the Latin for putting up a house — so it is strengthening of the inner kind.

clue.text: He's too drunk to be calm

indicators.note: A drunk man cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the line they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A man too far gone in drink to be talked down.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the clue's five words are the fodder, which leaves 'drunk' to do the shuffling and nothing spare. 'Calm' is the verb here, what you do to somebody, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To soothe a frightened child is to calm them, so the two verbs are plain synonyms taking the same sort of object.

clue.text: Eccles printed out game

indicators.note: Something out of true is not as it should be, so the letters it touches come out in an order other than their own.

parts.note: Eccles is the name at the top of this puzzle, and the setter referring to himself is I
anagram fodder, the other seven letters

explanation.surface: Eccles printing a game out at his desk.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter who names himself in a clue is asking for the letter I, and Eccles is the pseudonym this puzzle is signed with. 'Game' is the adjective, as in game for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody game for anything will take it on whatever the odds, which is what intrepid says of an explorer.

clue.text: Broadcaster with radical culture

parts.note: Sky is the satellite broadcaster that carries much of British television
R stands for a radical in a chemist's formula, the group left unnamed

explanation.surface: A television company with a radical streak running through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Culture' is the dairy sense, the bacteria that turn milk, rather than anything a broadcaster commissions. The answer is the thick soured milk Icelanders have eaten since Norse times, now sold in Britain as a high-protein yoghurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Skyr is the Icelandic soured-milk food set with a live starter, so 'culture' names it by the bacteria that make it what it is.

clue.text: Solitude: year wasted in a boring manner

indicators.note: A wasted evening has gone to pieces, and letters in pieces are put back in an order nobody chose.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
y is the year of a date or a mortgage term

explanation.surface: A year of solitude gone entirely to waste.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is the join, with fodder on both sides of it and the definition left at the end. 'Wasted' reads as the fate of the year and is the word doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done tediously drags on and bores whoever has to sit through it, which is doing it in a boring manner.
